items.method: conceptual analysis/commentary with demonstrations
items.finding: The paper argues that LLMs can generate original, coherent text that evades detection by software and trained staff, and that whether an integrity breach occurs depends on whether the student discloses AI use. It also notes potential support for writing education and EFL learners.
items.limitations: Not specific to graduate students; no systematic empirical sample described in abstract; conceptual.

items.method: research essay (non-systematic, conceptual)
items.finding: The essay discusses AI applications (chatbots, personalized learning, predictive analytics) for international students and argues they may improve learning efficiency. It identifies risks including privacy, cultural differences, language proficiency and ethics.
items.limitations: Conceptual essay without empirical data; focus on international students broadly rather than graduate research productivity or quality.

items.method: learning analytics study (HMM sequence analysis, process mining) of recorded interactions
items.sample: 10 doctoral students, 626 recorded activities
items.finding: Doctoral students who engaged in iterative, highly interactive processes with the GAI writing tool generally achieved better writing task performance, in contrast to those with other (less interactive) usage patterns. The study identifies distinct human-AI collaboration patterns in academic writing.
items.limitations: Very small sample (n=10) of doctoral students; single writing task and single tool; abstract is truncated.

items.method: researcher-conducted tests of ChatGPT (30 theory- and application-based tests)
items.sample: 30 ChatGPT tests
items.finding: ChatGPT was found to give accurate and reliable input and idea generation for students, but unethical use may lead to 'human unintelligence' and unlearning and make it harder for instructors to assess learning outcomes.
items.limitations: No human participants; focused on undergraduate-type communication and writing courses; small ad hoc test set.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: The review describes development and applications of LLMs in health care, noting potential in medical education and medical writing alongside challenges requiring supervision.
items.limitations: Focus on clinical/biomedical LLM applications; not about graduate students or research productivity; no review method described.

items.method: qualitative interview study
items.sample: lecturers (number not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Lecturers reported ChatGPT helps with finding information, ideas, translation and alternative questions, and they perceived it to improve productivity and learning efficiency, while stressing verification of its output.
items.limitations: Participants are lecturers, not graduate students; perceived (self-reported) productivity; sample size not stated.

items.method: survey n=284
items.sample: 284 UK academics
items.finding: Although generative AI was expected to relieve academic overwork, the survey of UK academics suggests the digitalisation of higher education work may not deliver such relief (abstract truncated). The paper frames GAI use within productivity pressure and audit culture.
items.limitations: Population is UK academics rather than graduate students; abstract truncated so findings are only partly visible.

items.method: cross-sectional survey with SEM (TAM-based)
items.sample: 262 students at King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia
items.finding: Interaction and collaborative learning and information quality drove ChatGPT adoption and continued use for research, with perceived ease of use and usefulness as mediators, influencing learning satisfaction.
items.limitations: Self-report questionnaire at a single university; measures satisfaction and adoption rather than productivity or research quality; not graduate-specific.

items.method: narrative review of LLMs in healthcare
items.finding: The paper reviews LLM architectures and medical training datasets and notes potential to accelerate medical research along with technical and ethical issues.
items.limitations: Healthcare/technical focus; not about graduate students; no review method stated.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: The review outlines opportunities of LLMs in medical education and notes risks of academic misconduct, overreliance on AI, diluted critical thinking, and inaccurate content.
items.limitations: Medical school context, not graduate research; narrative review without systematic method.

items.method: qualitative study (interviews/practices and perspectives)
items.sample: 20 Australian postgraduate research students with at least 4 months of ChatGPT use in research
items.finding: Students reported accelerated research progress, enhanced research quality, improved scholarly and professional skills, greater critical thinking, confidence and autonomy, and a deeper supervisory relationship. The findings suggest supervisor roles shift toward strategic, high-level guidance.
items.limitations: Small self-reported qualitative sample; single country; perceived rather than measured productivity or quality

items.method: randomized experiment with pre/post tests plus semi-structured interviews, n=60
items.sample: 60 postgraduate EFL students (25 interviewed from experimental group)
items.finding: The Grammarly AI-feedback group scored significantly higher on post-test writing than controls. Use of AI features correlated positively with revision frequency and improvements in content, organization, and cohesion.
items.limitations: Small sample; EFL writing proficiency rather than research output; Grammarly tool; short intervention

items.method: cross-sectional survey n=399
items.sample: 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from various disciplines in Hong Kong
items.finding: Students held generally positive attitudes toward GenAI and saw value in writing, brainstorming, and research and analysis support. They also raised concerns about accuracy, privacy, ethics, and effects on personal development.
items.limitations: Self-reported perceptions; mixed undergraduate and postgraduate sample; single city; no outcome measures

items.method: philosophical/conceptual argument
items.finding: The authors argue that LLM falsehoods are better understood as 'bullshit' in Frankfurt's sense, since the models are indifferent to the truth of their outputs.
items.limitations: Conceptual essay with no empirical data; not specific to graduate students

items.method: comparative performance analysis of LLMs against 11 human-conducted systematic reviews (33 prompts)
items.sample: 11 systematic reviews across 4 fields, 33 prompts to LLMs
items.finding: ChatGPT and Bard were tested on reproducing systematic-review reference lists, measured by recall, precision, F1-score, and hallucination rate. The abstract shown is truncated before the numerical results.
items.limitations: Narrow topic (rotator cuff pathology); early models; not tested on graduate students; results truncated in abstract

items.method: online survey with structural equation modeling, n=286
items.sample: 286 Austrian university students
items.finding: AI practical application positively influenced AI self-efficacy and AI output quality, while AI critical appraisal had a significant negative effect on both. The model also examined effects of self-efficacy and output quality on academic performance.
items.limitations: Cross-sectional self-report; general university students rather than graduate researchers; single country

items.method: systematic review of 33 empirical studies (485 screened)
items.sample: 33 empirical studies selected from 485 identified
items.finding: The review identifies five limitations of ChatGPT (accuracy and reliability, critical thinking, learning impacts, technical constraints, ethical and privacy concerns) and five opportunities, including workflow enhancement and content creation.
items.limitations: Not specific to graduate research; limited transparency on ChatGPT versions; uncertain transfer to newer models

items.method: mixed-methods randomized study with pre/post tests and interviews, n=50
items.sample: 50 international Chinese-as-a-second-language students (6 interviewed)
items.finding: ChatGPT-assisted learning supported knowledge acquisition, a supportive learning environment, and motivation in academic writing. Participants also raised concerns about over-reliance, ethics, technical issues, and unreliable AI content.
items.limitations: Small sample; language learners rather than graduate researchers; single university context

items.method: rapid literature review following PRISMA
items.finding: ChatGPT can support English language learning through meaning-focused input, scaffolding, feedback on accuracy, and fluency practice, and can help teachers with lesson planning and assessment. The abstract notes issues alongside the benefits but is truncated.
items.limitations: Rapid review; focused on English language teaching rather than graduate research; number of studies not stated in abstract

items.method: brief narrative review
items.finding: The review covers ChatGPT's technological underpinnings, features, applications, and impacts across domains, and outlines its strengths and limitations with recommendations for future research.
items.limitations: Narrative review with no stated method; general overview with no graduate-student focus

items.method: comparative study of 2 literature reviews (GPT-4 vs human-conducted)
items.sample: 2 literature reviews on physician-patient relational dynamics in medicolegal contexts
items.finding: The study compares the quality of a GPT-4-generated literature review, built with an iterative prompt engineering approach, against a human-led review on the same topic. The abstract is truncated and does not report the quality results.
items.limitations: Only two reviews compared; single topic; GPT-4 knowledge cutoff of September 2021; not specific to graduate students; results truncated in abstract

items.method: exploratory qualitative/conceptual exploration with a leadership research example
items.finding: ChatGPT use in undergraduate and postgraduate research supervision can support psychological need fulfilment, student autonomy and relatedness, and provide formative feedback. Limitations include weak handling of social injustice and context-appropriate content, and a tendency to reproduce current normative practices.
items.limitations: Method and sample not clearly described; single example from leadership research; mixes undergraduate and postgraduate contexts

items.method: content analysis of news articles (N=100)
items.sample: 100 news articles from Australia, New Zealand, the US and the UK
items.finding: News coverage of ChatGPT in higher education focuses mainly on academic integrity concerns and on innovative assessment design, with mixed university responses. Little public discussion addresses its potential to enhance student learning.
items.limitations: Based on news media rather than student data; not specific to graduate research; four countries only

items.method: systematic review of 41 studies
items.sample: 41 studies, 2021-2024, from ABI/INFORM, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore and JSTOR
items.finding: GenAI can enhance educational engagement and efficiency but also poses significant risks of academic dishonesty. The review suggests improving digital literacy and developing robust detection tools.
items.limitations: Limited database diversity; focuses on general higher education, not graduate research

items.method: questionnaire survey using the Technology Acceptance Model
items.sample: doctoral students in China (n not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Doctoral students showed a high intention to use ChatGPT in writing. Attitude predicted behavioural intention and mediated the effects of perceived usefulness and ease of use, and prior ChatGPT experience influenced perceived ease of use.
items.limitations: Measures acceptance and intention rather than productivity or quality outcomes; self-report; China only

items.method: online survey, N=505
items.sample: higher education students in Saudi Arabia (N=505)
items.finding: Participants reported positive attitudes and high awareness of GenAI in research, and beneficial experiences in expanding project scope and improving efficiency. They stressed the need for training and guidance, and raised ethical concerns about transparency and bias.
items.limitations: Self-reported perceptions; single country; student level mix not specified; no objective productivity measures

items.method: literature review plus survey of students and teachers
items.finding: Most participants argued that human teachers have unique qualities such as critical thinking, creativity and emotions that AI cannot replace. The paper recommends AI literacy and attention to data protection, ethics and privacy.
items.limitations: Focus on teachers' role rather than student research; sample not described; preprint

items.method: commentary/position paper
items.finding: The paper argues that GenAI increases plagiarism and cheating and that most institutions lack formal AI guidelines. It calls for clear institutional policies, AI literacy and ethics education.
items.limitations: No empirical method described in abstract; general college students, not graduate research

items.method: cross-sectional questionnaire survey with ANOVA
items.sample: 422 university students in Slovenia
items.finding: Students recognise the efficiency of AI tools but are concerned about impacts on learning quality and academic integrity. Usage was compared by level and field of study.
items.limitations: Self-report; single country; general university students rather than graduate researchers

items.method: quantitative survey (details unclear from abstract)
items.finding: The study examines higher education students' awareness, adoption patterns, perceived benefits and challenges of GenAI, including ethical concerns, reliability and accessibility. The abstract does not report specific results.
items.limitations: Abstract lacks sample size and results; general students, not graduate-specific

items.method: cross-sectional survey with structural equation modeling
items.sample: university students (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Network quality, accessibility and system responsiveness contributed to satisfaction. Satisfaction, organizational culture, social influence and knowledge application significantly affected intention to adopt ChatGPT.
items.limitations: Measures adoption intention rather than research productivity or quality; undergraduate/general students rather than graduate researchers; cross-sectional and self-report.

items.method: narrative review with thematic analysis of 40 empirical studies
items.sample: 40 peer-reviewed empirical studies on ChatGPT adoption in higher education
items.finding: Hedonic motivation, usability, perceived benefits, system responsiveness and relative advantage were confirmed adoption factors. Effects of social influence, facilitating conditions, privacy and security varied.
items.limitations: Concerns adoption and acceptance, not research outcomes; not specific to graduate students; narrative synthesis.

items.method: analytical paper with demonstrated example attacks (jailbreaks, prompt injection) on ChatGPT
items.finding: Shows that ChatGPT can be exploited via jailbreaks, reverse psychology and prompt injection, and that GenAI can be used to build cyber attacks such as social engineering and phishing.
items.limitations: Cybersecurity focus; unrelated to graduate research productivity or quality.

items.method: quantitative study with moderation analysis (survey implied)
items.sample: 500 students across science, engineering, humanities and social sciences faculties
items.finding: Adaptive learning technologies, personalized feedback and interactive AI tools improved student engagement. Students with higher digital literacy engaged more with digital tools.
items.limitations: Outcome is engagement, not research productivity or quality; general students, not graduate researchers; abstract describes digital literacy inconsistently as mediating and moderating.

items.method: course-based qualitative study using interactive and reflective data on a self-regulated learning micro-curriculum
items.sample: 60 PhD students at a Swedish university
items.finding: Doctoral students started with varied attitudes and limited knowledge of GAI. After the micro-curriculum they showed de-enchantment with GAI, better understanding of ethical issues, developed prompting methods and greater awareness of text ownership.
items.limitations: Single institution and single course; self-reported reflections; no productivity or quality measures.

items.method: systematic review (PRISMA) of 26 articles
items.sample: 26 articles on ChatGPT in academic writing, personalized learning and coding
items.finding: ChatGPT supports academic writing through error detection and content refinement and assists coding with explanations and reusable snippets. The abstract also indicates limitations, but they are truncated.
items.limitations: Higher education generally, not graduate students; small number of studies; abstract truncated.

items.method: observational study with mediation and moderation analysis
items.sample: 6986 executives (LinkedIn data) and firm 10-K statements
items.finding: Top management AI literacy positively affected firm AI orientation and AI implementation ability. The effect was stronger in startups than in incumbents.
items.limitations: Corporate executives and firms, not graduate students; observational data.

items.method: cross-sectional survey with structural equation modeling
items.sample: 455 Chinese college students
items.finding: Career self-efficacy negatively predicted job-seeking anxiety, with AI attitudes and AI literacy as significant mediators.
items.limitations: Focuses on job-seeking anxiety, not research productivity or quality; undergraduates; cross-sectional.

items.method: comparison of AI tools and a proposed theoretical framework
items.finding: Compares responsive AI tools for tourism and proposes a GAI-based decision-making framework for itinerary creation and traveler interaction.
items.limitations: Tourism industry; conceptual framework; off-topic.

items.method: scale development and validation with mediation analysis
items.sample: employees (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Developed a five-dimension Generative AI Literacy scale. GenAI literacy positively affected job performance (β = 0.680, p < 0.001), partially mediated by creative self-efficacy (indirect effect = 0.537).
items.limitations: Workplace employees, not graduate students; job performance rather than research outcomes.

items.method: observational study with retrospective think-aloud interviews and questionnaires, n=27
items.sample: 27 undergraduate non-expert ChatGPT users (M age = 20.37)
items.finding: The study categorizes the strategies students used with ChatGPT in a source-based writing task and relates them to the quality and content of their written products. The abstract is truncated, so the specific results are not available.
items.limitations: Small sample of undergraduates, not graduate students; abstract truncated before results; single task.

items.method: policy framework proposal drawing on consultative experiences of two Australian universities
items.finding: The authors propose a principles-based university framework for responsible AI use in research, built on honesty, transparency and accountability. It is meant to underpin training, communication, infrastructure and process change.
items.limitations: Conceptual framework from two universities; no empirical evaluation of outcomes; not specific to graduate students.

items.method: cross-sectional survey n=405 with t-tests and linear regression
items.sample: 405 undergraduate students (STEM vs non-STEM)
items.finding: STEM students rated GenAI's support for critical thinking significantly higher than non-STEM peers, while creativity perceptions did not differ by discipline. AI self-efficacy significantly predicted perceived critical-thinking and creativity support.
items.limitations: Undergraduate sample; self-reported perceptions rather than measured outcomes; cross-sectional design.

items.method: qualitative study with survey questionnaires and short interviews, n=25
items.sample: 25 postgraduate English-major students at Industrial University of Ho Chi Minh City
items.finding: The study reports that the challenges of using ChatGPT in academic writing outweigh its benefits for these postgraduate students. It also notes concern about over-reliance.
items.limitations: Small single-institution sample; self-reported data; English majors only; focuses on disadvantages.

items.method: mixed-methods study (surveys and interviews, ANOVA, correlation, thematic analysis) n=666
items.sample: 666 participants across diverse ages and educational backgrounds
items.finding: Frequent AI tool use correlated negatively with critical thinking, mediated by cognitive offloading. Younger participants showed higher AI dependence and lower critical thinking scores.
items.limitations: General population rather than graduate researchers; correlational design; self-report.

items.method: scale development survey (n=165) and three-wave time-lagged survey (n=494)
items.sample: 165 and 494 university students in two studies
items.finding: Higher academic workload and time pressure led students to use ChatGPT more. The study also examined usage effects on procrastination, memory loss and academic performance, though the abstract is truncated before those results.
items.limitations: University students generally, not graduate researchers; self-reported measures; abstract truncated.

items.method: systematic literature review of 53 peer-reviewed articles (Scopus, Web of Science, 2020-2024)
items.sample: 53 articles
items.finding: GenAI improves personalized feedback and accessibility but introduces risks such as loss of cognitive autonomy, misuse of student data and weak regulatory oversight. The review calls for regulatory frameworks and pedagogical strategies.
items.limitations: Covers education broadly rather than graduate research; thematic synthesis of mostly conceptual work.

items.method: bibliometric analysis of 47 Scopus papers
items.sample: 47 research papers
items.finding: Research on ChatGPT in higher education clusters around academic integrity, learning environment, student engagement and scholarly research, with the US most productive. Academic integrity and research are heavily studied.
items.limitations: Bibliometric mapping with no outcome data; small corpus from one database; not graduate-specific.

items.method: critical essay
items.finding: The essay argues that generative AI poses a threat and an opportunity for the accounting academy and accounting education. It calls for renewed focus on the human and critical dimensions of accounting.
items.limitations: Opinion piece with no empirical data; focused on accounting education rather than graduate research.

items.method: structured dialectical dialogue (commentary)
items.finding: The article presents opposing views on AI in higher education research, highlighting tensions between efficiency and ethical or epistemological integrity. It offers no resolution and no empirical findings.
items.limitations: Non-empirical opinion/dialogue piece; not specific to graduate students.

items.method: cross-sectional survey n=393
items.sample: 393 undergraduate and postgraduate students across disciplines
items.finding: Students clearly disapprove of direct AI content generation but are ambivalent about subtler AI uses. The study introduces a novel instrument for measuring perceptions of AI-giarism.
items.limitations: Mixed undergraduate/postgraduate sample; perceptions rather than behaviours or outcomes; not graduate-specific.

items.method: mixed methods: questionnaire survey n=475 plus interviews n=12
items.sample: 475 survey respondents and 12 interviewees at two Chinese universities
items.finding: Students generally view GenAI positively for learning academic communication, especially writing, grammar, vocabulary and reading, though the abstract notes limitations and challenges.
items.limitations: Self-reported perceptions; two universities in China; students not restricted to graduate level; no measured productivity or quality outcomes.

items.method: systematic review (PRISMA) of 38 studies
items.sample: 38 studies selected from 3,214 identified documents (2022–2024)
items.finding: 71.4% of studies reported a positive role of GenAI in self-regulated learning and 62.5% in critical thinking, though researchers cautioned against overreliance that could reduce independent thinking.
items.limitations: General student population rather than graduate researchers; focus on learning skills, not research output; reports vote-count percentages.

items.method: mixed-methods study (quantitative and qualitative) leading to policy framework development
items.sample: 457 students and 180 teachers and staff in Hong Kong universities
items.finding: Proposes an AI Ecological Education Policy Framework with Pedagogical, Governance and Operational dimensions for university use of text-generative AI.
items.limitations: Hong Kong universities only; focus on teaching and learning generally, not graduate research.

items.method: thing ethnography (qualitative, ChatGPT as informant)
items.finding: ChatGPT's own account of higher education challenges stresses academic integrity, plagiarism detection and critical thinking, and the need for clear policies and guidelines. The study calls for empirical research on user experiences.
items.limitations: Findings are generated by the AI itself, not by empirical observation of users; no graduate focus; no outcome measurement.

items.method: expert commentary (nine contributors)
items.finding: GenAI can enhance learning design, regulation of learning, feedback and assessment, but poses limitations, ethical concerns and risk of misuse. The authors call for policy, support and competence mechanisms and stronger evidence.
items.limitations: Commentary without empirical data; general education focus, not graduate research.

items.method: randomised controlled experiment n=1625
items.sample: 1625 students across 10 courses
items.finding: Tests whether students keep their behaviour once AI assistance is removed or instead continue relying on it, in the context of peer feedback. The abstract is truncated, so the results are not shown.
items.limitations: Peer-review context, not graduate research; AI is not generative; results truncated in the abstract.

items.method: systematic review (PRISMA) with bibliometric analysis of 355 papers
items.sample: 355 included papers from Scopus (625 identified)
items.finding: Identifies a lack of agreed guidelines on GenAI use in higher education. Research gaps include detection of AI-generated text and incorporation of GenAI into curriculum and assessment.
items.limitations: Scopus only; bibliometric mapping rather than effect synthesis; teaching and learning focus.

items.method: systematic literature review (PRISMA) of 37 studies
items.sample: 37 articles from Scopus and Web of Science (Jan 2023–Jan 2024)
items.finding: Studies cluster around GAI applications, stakeholder acceptance and specific use situations. Challenges include assessment practices, institutional strategies and academic integrity risks.
items.limitations: Short review window; general higher education rather than graduate research.

items.method: content analysis of 5 international documents and policy documents from 30 universities
items.sample: 30 top-500 universities (May–July 2023) and 5 UN/EU/OECD documents
items.finding: University policies emphasise that student work must reflect individual knowledge and that humans retain responsibility for AI-related wrongdoing. Instructors are given flexibility in how they use GenAI in their courses.
items.limitations: Early policy snapshot from top-ranked universities only; focuses on coursework rather than graduate research.

items.method: cross-sectional survey, n=982 students and 76 faculty
items.sample: 982 students and 76 faculty at one large public US university, Fall 2023
items.finding: Students and faculty did not differ significantly in attitudes toward GenAI, except for ease of use, hedonic motivation, habit, and interest in new technologies. Regular use was low in both groups, and attitudes differed between males in STEM majors and females in non-STEM majors.
items.limitations: Single institution, mostly undergraduate coursework context rather than graduate research, self-reported perceptions, abstract truncated; no productivity or quality outcomes.

items.method: cross-sectional online survey with PLS-SEM, TPB framework
items.sample: 130 lecturers and 168 students in higher education institutions across several countries
items.finding: Perceived strengths and advantages of GenAI positively affect attitudes, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control, which in turn raise intention to use GenAI and actual usage. Lecturers and students perceive risks and weaknesses differently.
items.limitations: Adoption-focused rather than productivity or quality outcomes; self-reported; not specific to graduate students or research

items.method: qualitative literature review (narrative, no stated systematic method)
items.finding: AI in higher education may improve productivity and efficiency, but raises concerns about plagiarism, weakened critical thinking, suppressed creativity and eroded originality in research and scholarship.
items.limitations: Narrative review with limited methodological detail; general higher education, not graduate research specifically

items.method: inductive thematic analysis of publisher policies, AI-assisted and manual
items.sample: policies of leading academic publishers and other publishing or academic entities (number not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Analysis of publisher AI policies yielded six themes, three identified independently by both the AI-assisted and manual analyses, reflecting a lack of cohesive guidelines on authorship, integrity and research methods.
items.limitations: Policy document analysis; sample size not stated in abstract; abstract truncated; does not address graduate students directly

items.method: qualitative study: email interviews, focus groups, WhatsApp discussions
items.sample: lecturers, students and markers in a distance learning academic writing module (exact numbers not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Findings indicate generative AI has a positive potential impact on academic writing teaching and learning and on student motivation to improve writing.
items.limitations: Qualitative perceptions only; single institution; focus on writing skills in a course, not graduate research output; found_for rq5 but little on risks

items.method: case studies of 6 commercial AI products
items.sample: 6 commercial products in the creative industries
items.finding: AI products were more labour intensive than traditional media products, human contributions were invisibilised, and there was potential for labour displacement in the ideation phase.
items.limitations: Creative industries labour context; unrelated to graduate students or academic research

items.method: peer interviews with thematic analysis
items.sample: 106 first-year undergraduates and 81 first-year postgraduates at one East China university
items.finding: Grade was the most influential factor in perceptions of ChatGPT, followed by age and major. Postgraduates showed greater awareness of ChatGPT's limitations for academic problems and more concern about security issues.
items.limitations: Single university; first-year students only; perceptions rather than measured productivity or quality outcomes

items.method: cross-sectional survey
items.sample: 401 students from major U.S. universities
items.finding: Students' ethical beliefs, not institutional policy awareness, were the strongest predictors of perceived misconduct and actual AI use in writing. Policy awareness had no significant effect on ethical judgments or behaviour.
items.limitations: Self-reported survey; students not limited to graduate level; no productivity or quality outcome measures

items.method: qualitative open-ended questionnaires with thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke)
items.sample: 16 lecturers
items.finding: Lecturers use strategies such as AI-detection tools like Turnitin and innovative assessment to uphold academic integrity while promoting responsible AI use in personalised learning.
items.limitations: Small sample, self-reported data, context-specific; lecturers' view of teaching, not graduate research

items.method: brief overview/commentary
items.finding: Overviews ChatGPT capabilities and common uses for medical writing, lists generative AI and detection tools, and gives recommendations for policymakers, information professionals and medical faculty on constructive use and integrity.
items.limitations: Brief non-empirical overview; medical field focus; no outcome data

items.method: narrative review of research, theoretical frameworks and case studies (method not detailed)
items.finding: Discusses concerns that overreliance on AI may reduce motivation for self-directed analysis, diminish cognitive effort and weaken critical thinking, while noting AI's potential for personalised learning and efficiency.
items.limitations: No stated review method; general students rather than graduate researchers; abstract gives no quantitative results

items.method: qualitative semi-structured interviews, thematic analysis
items.sample: recently graduated management students (number not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Students perceived ChatGPT positively for individual use, citing immediacy, reassurance and potential to augment performance and creativity. They raised concerns about equitable access, devaluation of degrees, and academic misconduct in group work, with integrity problematic given absent institutional transparency and clear policy.
items.limitations: Qualitative with likely small sample; management graduates, not research-focused graduate students; perceptions rather than measured outcomes

items.method: cross-sectional online survey n=482
items.sample: 482 higher education students across diverse institutions, primarily in the US
items.finding: A significant majority of students felt comfortable using GenAI and recognized its potential to enhance productivity and academic success. They also reported concerns about academic integrity, overreliance on AI, and data privacy and security, with demographic differences in perceived readiness, benefits and challenges.
items.limitations: Self-reported perceptions; general student population rather than graduate researchers; no measured productivity or quality outcomes

items.method: narrative review with author-run ChatGPT coding experiments
items.finding: Outlines opportunities (personalized feedback, accessibility) and threats (cheating, reduced critical thinking, difficulty evaluating output) of ChatGPT in education and research, with coding experiments (code generation, pseudocode, code correction) for programming learning.
items.limitations: General education focus, not graduate students; no formal systematic method stated; abstract truncated.

items.method: meta-analysis of 51 studies (retracted article)
items.sample: 51 research studies published Nov 2022-Feb 2025
items.finding: Reported large positive effect of ChatGPT on learning performance (g=0.867) and moderate effects on learning perception (g=0.456) and higher-order thinking (g=0.457), moderated by course type, learning model and duration.
items.limitations: Article is retracted, so results are unreliable; concerns general students rather than graduate researchers; learning outcomes not research output.

items.method: benchmark evaluation on new curated datasets (GHOSTS, miniGHOSTS)
items.sample: graduate-level mathematics datasets curated by working mathematicians; ChatGPT (Jan 2023 versions) and GPT-4
items.finding: Benchmarks ChatGPT and GPT-4 on graduate-level natural-language mathematics across multiple dimensions of reasoning, testing whether they can assist professional mathematicians.
items.limitations: Tests model capability, not graduate student users or their productivity; early model versions; abstract truncated.

items.method: evaluation study with reviewer ratings, ANOVA and thematic analysis
items.sample: 4 ChatGPT-generated articles evaluated by 23 reviewers; 50 ChatGPT-generated abstracts
items.finding: Assessed the quality of ChatGPT-generated research articles and abstracts for research framework, data analysis and literature review, and explored concerns about ownership and research integrity.
items.limitations: Small number of generated articles; not graduate students as users; results not shown in the abstract.

items.method: systematic review with thematic analysis
items.finding: Synthesizes literature into positive and negative themes of ChatGPT integration in education, including potential negative impacts on educational processes.
items.limitations: Broad education focus, not graduate research; number of studies not stated in abstract; early literature.

items.method: quasi-experimental mixed-methods study
items.sample: 82 college students in two classes (ChatGPT-facilitated vs self-directed programming)
items.finding: Students in ChatGPT-facilitated programming mode showed different behaviors, such as more debugging, copying and pasting code, and reading feedback, than the self-directed group.
items.limitations: Undergraduate programming context, not graduate research; single course; abstract truncated.

items.method: semi-structured interviews with content analysis
items.sample: 15 higher education students
items.finding: Five categories of task motivation emerged (task enjoyment, reported effort, result assessment, perceived relevance, interaction), with more positive than negative motivational characteristics when learning with ChatGPT.
items.limitations: Small sample; learning motivation rather than research productivity or quality; self-reported.

items.method: RCT n=26
items.sample: 26 prospective physics teacher students
items.finding: Task correctness did not differ between ChatGPT and textbook groups, but textbook users produced clearer, more contextually embedded tasks; both groups struggled with task specificity.
items.limitations: Very small sample; prospective teachers, not graduate researchers; task development rather than research output.

items.method: three case studies (experimental reflective lab)
items.sample: undergraduate and postgraduate ICT students (n not stated)
items.finding: Students perceived ChatGPT as useful and enjoyable, and performance on functionality, user flow and content comprehension appeared better than with traditional search engines.
items.limitations: Sample size not stated; perception-based; mixed undergraduate/postgraduate in classroom tasks rather than research.

items.method: three-session intervention study with prompt-behavior profile analysis
items.sample: students in programming learning (n not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Five AI-interaction profiles were identified, and profile distribution changed significantly across interventions (no guidance, prompt training, lab guide with sample prompts) and related to learning performance.
items.limitations: Programming learning context, not graduate research; sample size unclear; abstract truncated.

items.method: systematic review (number of studies not stated in abstract)
